SMSD

SMSD (Sequential Methods for Study Design) is for researchers who have to plan a study without knowing the population values that a sample size formula asks for: a standard deviation, a correlation, or the effect size itself. A sequential procedure does not guess them. Data are collected in stages, and after each stage a stopping rule computed from the data in hand says whether the goal has been reached. The goal can be a confidence interval as narrow as requested (accuracy in parameter estimation, AIPE), an estimate whose combined cost of estimation error and of sampling is as small as it can be made (minimum risk point estimation, MRPE), or the most precise estimate of a contrast that a fixed budget can buy. The methods are general; the articles that developed them have psychology, education, management, and related fields in view. The confidence interval procedures for effect sizes assume no particular distribution for the data, with the exception of the one for the squared multiple correlation.

Installation 

# The released version, from CRAN
install.packages("SMSD")

# Or the development version, from GitHub (one of the two, not both)
# install.packages("remotes")
# remotes::install_github("yelleKneK/SMSD")

Install the source tarball identified by the release record when you need this exact version. A CRAN mirror or the public GitHub branch can serve a different version, so verify packageVersion("SMSD") after installation. The tarball can be installed with install.packages("SMSD_1.0.0.tar.gz", repos = NULL, type = "source"); install its required dependencies first. The package needs DMAR 1.0.0 or later and R 4.0.0 or later.

For the replication of published examples, see vignette("published-examples", package = "SMSD"). For measured coverage, sample sizes, and figures from difficult designs, see vignette("coverage-and-design", package = "SMSD").

Where to Start

Start with seq_aipe_smd(), the standardized mean difference between two groups. Suppose a training program is compared with a control condition on employee engagement, and the aim is a 95% confidence interval for the standardized mean difference that is no wider than 0.60. The pilot function gives the first sample size, and the check function says whether sampling can stop. (The data are simulated, with a true difference of 0.4 standard deviations, so that the example runs on its own.)

library(SMSD)
set.seed(113)
trained <- rnorm(seq_aipe_smd_pilot(width = 0.60), mean = 4.9)
control <- rnorm(seq_aipe_smd_pilot(width = 0.60), mean = 4.5)
seq_aipe_smd(trained, control, width = 0.60)
#> Sequential check (standardized mean difference)
#> 
#>   Current n       : 7
#>   Criterion n     : 91
#>   Target width    : 0.6
#>   Confidence level: 95%
#>   Coverage        : asymptotic; assess with sensitivity analysis
#> 
#>   lower_limit       : -1.143786
#>   smd               : -0.1011596
#>   upper_limit       : 0.9414664
#>   xi_squared        : 1.980884
#>   criterion_n       : 91
#>   current_n         : 7
#> 
#>   Stopping rule met: FALSE

With the pilot sample of 7 people per group the rule is not met: the criterion asks for 91 per group as things stand, and that number is updated at every check. A study therefore adds participants and checks again, until the rule is met. seq_report() then writes the result up.

out <- seq_aipe_smd(trained, control, width = 0.60)
while (!attr(out, "is_satisfied")) {
  trained <- c(trained, rnorm(1, mean = 4.9))
  control <- c(control, rnorm(1, mean = 4.5))
  out <- seq_aipe_smd(trained, control, width = 0.60)
}
seq_report(out)
#> Sample size was determined with the sequential accuracy in parameter
#> estimation procedure for the standardized mean difference (Kelley,
#> Darku, & Chattopadhyay, 2018), with a target full width of 0.6 for the
#> 95% confidence interval. The stopping rule was met at n = 85 per group.
#> At that sample size the estimate of the standardized mean difference
#> was 0.356, 95% CI [0.058, 0.655]. The confidence level is asymptotic;
#> meeting the width target does not establish nominal coverage at this
#> sample size.
#> 
#> Reference
#> Kelley, K., Darku, F. B., & Chattopadhyay, B. (2018). Accuracy in
#>     parameter estimation for a general class of effect sizes: A
#>     sequential approach. Psychological Methods, 23(2), 226–243.
#>     doi:10.1037/met0000127

The final interval is 0.596 wide (computed from the limits before they are rounded for the report), within the 0.60 requested, and it contains the 0.4 used to generate the data. The check function does not prompt and keeps nothing between calls: the loop belongs to the study, and each call is a calculation on the data collected so far. For data already in hand, seq_path() runs the same loop in one call and plot() draws it. vignette("introduction", package = "SMSD") is the overview, and vignette("step-by-step-sequential-workflow", package = "SMSD") follows one study from its pilot sample to its stopping point.

A fixed width interval for a mean seq_fwd_norm_mean(), seq_fwd_dfr_mean(); in two stages, ts_fwd_norm_mean(), ts_fwd_dfr_mean() Mukhopadhyay & de Silva (2009)
The location of a negative exponential distribution seq_fwd_nexp_mean(), ts_fwd_nexp_mean(), seq_mr_nexp_mean() Mukhopadhyay & de Silva (2009)

The final sample size and risk to expect seq_mr_cv_sensitivity(), seq_mr_smd_sensitivity() The article of the procedure simulated

Reading and Reporting a Result
The result of one check print(), summary(), generics::tidy(), generics::glance() This package

Each of the 25 check functions has a companion that returns its pilot sample size and is named by adding _pilot, as in seq_aipe_smd_pilot(). In all, the package exports 74 functions, 11 of them _sensitivity() functions. help("SMSD-package") lists every one of them with a link.

The seq_aipe_* functions take the full width of the interval as width. The classical interval procedures take d, and what d measures depends on the procedure: the half width of the interval for a mean (seq_fwd_norm_mean(), seq_fwd_dfr_mean(), ts_fwd_norm_mean(), ts_fwd_dfr_mean()), the full width for the location of a negative exponential distribution (seq_fwd_nexp_mean(), ts_fwd_nexp_mean()), and half of the largest length allowed for the interval for a median (seq_blci_dfr_median()). Likewise gamma has two meanings. In seq_mr_cv(), seq_mr_smd(), seq_mr_dfr_mean_arb(), and their pilot functions it is the exponent of the correction term n−γ in the stopping rule; in the other pilot functions of the classical procedures it is a constant of the pilot rule that sets the size of the pilot sample. Each help page says which.

What the Procedures Guarantee

The seq_aipe_* procedures deliver the requested width by construction: when the stopping rule is met, the interval is no wider than the target. Coverage is a different matter. Under the relevant regularity conditions, it is an asymptotic property, reached as the target narrows and the final sample grows, and it can fall well short of the confidence level in the small samples that a wide target, a strong relationship, or many predictors produce. The sensitivity functions show what to expect before any data are collected. Each row below is one call.

G <- 2000
runs <- list(
  "Standardized mean difference of 0.5, width 0.8" =
    seq_aipe_smd_sensitivity(0.5, width = 0.8, G = G, seed = 113),
  "Pearson correlation of 0.4, width 0.4" =
    seq_aipe_r_sensitivity(0.4, width = 0.4, G = G, seed = 113),
  "Pearson correlation of 0.8, width 0.4" =
    seq_aipe_r_sensitivity(0.8, width = 0.4, G = G, seed = 113),
  "Regression slope of 0.5, width 0.4" =
    seq_aipe_reg_coef_sensitivity(0.5, width = 0.4, G = G, seed = 113),
  "Coefficient of variation of 0.5, lognormal data, width 0.2" =
    seq_aipe_cv_sensitivity(0.5, width = 0.2, distribution = "lognormal",
                            G = G, seed = 113),
  "Squared multiple correlation of 0.5, 5 predictors, width 0.3" =
    seq_aipe_R2_sensitivity(0.5, width = 0.3, p = 5, G = G, seed = 113),
  "Squared multiple correlation of 0.5, 15 predictors, width 0.3" =
    seq_aipe_R2_sensitivity(0.5, width = 0.3, p = 15, G = G, seed = 113)
)
row_of <- function(term) vapply(runs, function(run) run$value[run$term == term], 0)
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(names(runs), row_of("mean_n"), row_of("pct_width_within"),
             row_of("coverage")),
  digits = c(0, 0, 0, 2), row.names = FALSE,
  col.names = c("Design", "Mean final sample size",
                "Intervals within the width (%)", "Coverage of the 95% interval")
)
Design Mean final sample size Intervals within the width (%) Coverage of the 95% interval
Standardized mean difference of 0.5, width 0.8 50 100 0.94
Pearson correlation of 0.4, width 0.4 56 100 0.78
Pearson correlation of 0.8, width 0.4 23 100 0.70
Regression slope of 0.5, width 0.4 82 100 0.84
Coefficient of variation of 0.5, lognormal data, width 0.2 63 100 0.79
Squared multiple correlation of 0.5, 5 predictors, width 0.3 82 100 0.85
Squared multiple correlation of 0.5, 15 predictors, width 0.3 52 100 0.36

Every interval in every row was within its target width. Coverage was close to the nominal level for the standardized mean difference (0.94, with a Monte Carlo standard error of 0.005) and well below it in the other rows, from 0.85 down to 0.36 for the squared multiple correlation with 15 predictors. For the Pearson correlation it was lower for the strong relationship (0.70) than for the moderate one (0.78). Each figure comes from 2,000 simulated studies and has a Monte Carlo standard error of at most 0.011, so another run of the same design, such as the one a help page reports, can differ from it in the second decimal. (The sample sizes count observations per group for the standardized mean difference, pairs for the correlation and the slope, and observations otherwise.) A narrower target, which means a larger study, brings coverage toward the nominal level under those regularity conditions; a larger minimum pilot sample (m_0) can help as well. The null multiple R-squared boundary is an exception: increasing the sample size does not restore the Wald interval’s nominal coverage. The installed vignette vignette("coverage-and-design") explains this boundary and compares normal model reference intervals. The help page of each seq_aipe_* function states what its guarantee is and reports what was measured for it, and ?seq_aipe_sensitivity has a table over more conditions.

In a small sample the variance estimate that a stopping rule needs can be zero, negative, or not finite. The check functions then report the rule as not met, with a note, and sampling continues. This is a deliberate departure from the rules as printed in the articles, under which the study would stop at once with an interval far narrower than requested; the section “An Unusable Variance Estimate” of help("SMSD-package") describes it.

The classical procedures state their guarantees on their help pages as well. Some are exact: Stein’s two stage interval, ts_fwd_norm_mean(), covers a normal mean with at least the stated probability for any first stage. Others are asymptotic: the distribution free two stage interval, ts_fwd_dfr_mean(), covers a normal mean with probability 0.940 at a nominal 0.95 when the first stage has 30 observations and the target is narrow, and with less for skewed data.

Validation

  • Tests that pin published values. The test suite (37 test files) compares the package with numbers printed in the source articles: rows of Tables 2, 3, and 4 of Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay (2018); rows of Tables 2, 10, 11, 13, and 14 of Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay (2019); the worked examples and rows of Table 1 of Chattopadhyay and Kelley (2016) and of Table 3 of Chattopadhyay and Kelley (2017); and the allocation example and Table 1 of Chattopadhyay, Bandyopadhyay, Kelley, and Padalunkal (2025). One published row is not reproduced in full, and its test records the difference: for Kendall’s tau (Table 8 of the 2019 article) coverage and interval width are close to the article’s, but the mean final sample size runs about 2 percent above the published one and varies nearly twice as much from study to study. The cause is not resolved. Where no table exists, a procedure is run to its stopping point and compared with its theoretical sample size or its exact guarantee.
  • A cached simulation study. A study of the standardized mean difference and Pearson correlation procedures under normal and skewed data (18 conditions, 10,000 replications each) is installed with the package, at system.file("extdata", "aipe_simulation_results.rds", package = "SMSD"), and is displayed and discussed in vignette("complete-tour", package = "SMSD"). The script that produces it is in the data-raw folder of the source repository.
  • Two notes on departures from the articles as printed. The variance of the standardized mean difference corrects an omitted factor of 1/2 in Equation 26 of Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay (2018). The correction is installed with the package (system.file("eq26_correction.pdf", package = "SMSD")) and is posted by the authors at https://kenkelley.org/wp-content/uploads/articles/Kelley_Darku_Chattopadhyay_Equation_26.pdf. In seq_mr_cv() the variance of the coefficient of variation is by default the estimator of Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay (2018), which is consistent for any distribution with a finite fourth moment. Equation 22 of Chattopadhyay and Kelley (2016) agrees with it for normal data, and for any population with no excess kurtosis, and can differ otherwise; variance = "published" uses that equation, so that the article can be reproduced. The derivation is in a note installed with the package (system.file("cv_variance_note.md", package = "SMSD")), and ?seq_mr_cv summarizes it.
  • A comparison with the published tables. The validation article of the package website (vignettes/articles/validation.Rmd in the source repository) sets the package’s results beside the published ones, table by table.

How to Cite

citation("SMSD") gives the package entry and the six articles listed here, and toBibtex(citation("SMSD")) gives them as BibTeX entries. Please cite the package and the article that developed the method you used. The book is the source of the classical procedures.

  • Chattopadhyay, B., Bandyopadhyay, T., Kelley, K., & Padalunkal, J. J. (2025). A sequential approach for noninferiority or equivalence of a linear contrast under cost constraints. Psychological Methods, 30(2), 425–439. doi:10.1037/met0000570
  • Chattopadhyay, B., & De, S. K. (2016). Estimation of Gini index within pre-specified error bound. Econometrics, 4(3), 30. doi:10.3390/econometrics4030030
  • Chattopadhyay, B., & Kelley, K. (2016). Estimation of the coefficient of variation with minimum risk: A sequential method for minimizing sampling error and study cost. Multivariate Behavioral Research, 51(5), 627–648. doi:10.1080/00273171.2016.1203279
  • Chattopadhyay, B., & Kelley, K. (2017). Estimating the standardized mean difference with minimum risk: Maximizing accuracy and minimizing cost with sequential estimation. Psychological Methods, 22(1), 94–113. doi:10.1037/met0000089
  • Kelley, K., Darku, F. B., & Chattopadhyay, B. (2018). Accuracy in parameter estimation for a general class of effect sizes: A sequential approach. Psychological Methods, 23(2), 226–243. doi:10.1037/met0000127
  • Kelley, K., Darku, F. B., & Chattopadhyay, B. (2019). Sequential accuracy in parameter estimation for population correlation coefficients. Psychological Methods, 24(4), 492–515. doi:10.1037/met0000203
  • Mukhopadhyay, N., & de Silva, B. M. (2009). Sequential methods and their applications. Chapman & Hall/CRC. ISBN:9780367386535
